title: Function Pointers, Callbacks and Command-Line Arguments
summary: Functions live in memory too, so a pointer can refer to one. A **function pointer** lets you pass "which function to call" as an argument: a **callback**. Modern C++ mostly uses lambdas, but C interfaces use function pointers. Also here: reading a program's command-line arguments.
markdown:
## A pointer to a function A compiled function is a block of machine code at some address. A **function pointer** holds that address. ```cpp #include int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } int multiply(int a, int b) { return a * b; } int main() { int (*op)(int, int){ &add }; std::cout << op(3, 4) << '\n'; // 7 op = &multiply; std::cout << op(3, 4) << '\n'; // 12 return 0; } ``` The same line `op(3, 4)` does different things depending on where `op` points. ### Reading the declaration ``` int (*op) (int, int) │ │ └── called with two ints │ └── op is a pointer └── to a function returning int ``` The parentheses around `*op` are required. Without them, `int *op(int, int)` declares a function that returns an `int*`. An alias makes it bearable: ```cpp using BinaryOp = int (*)(int, int); BinaryOp op{ add }; ``` A function's name converts to a pointer automatically, so the `&` is optional. ## Callbacks A **callback** is a function you hand to other code for it to call when needed. It lets a general routine leave one decision to its caller. ```cpp bool ascending(int a, int b) { return a > b; } // "is this pair out of order?" bool descending(int a, int b) { return a < b; } void selectionSort(std::vector& v, bool (*outOfOrder)(int, int)) { for (std::size_t i{ 0 }; i < v.size(); ++i) { for (std::size_t j{ i + 1 }; j < v.size(); ++j) { if (outOfOrder(v[i], v[j])) { std::swap(v[i], v[j]); } } } } ``` ```cpp selectionSort(numbers, ascending); selectionSort(numbers, descending); selectionSort(numbers, [](int a, int b) { return a % 2 > b % 2; }); ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR C["selectionSort(v, descending)"] --> S["the sorting loop
knows nothing about order"] S -->|"asks: outOfOrder(a, b)?"| CB["descending"] CB -->|"true or false"| S ``` One sort, any ordering. This is exactly how the comparator of `std::sort` works. The last call passes a lambda. A lambda that **captures nothing** converts to a function pointer. One that captures cannot, because it carries data and a bare address has nowhere to keep it. ### Three ways to accept a callable | | Function pointer | `std::function` | Template or `auto` parameter | |---|---|---|---| | Accepts ordinary functions | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Accepts capturing lambdas | No | Yes | Yes | | Cost per call | Very small | Small | None: the call can be inlined | | Typical use | C interfaces | Storing callbacks | Algorithms | In your own code, prefer a template or `std::function` ([[5.07 Lambdas]]). Use function pointers when a C library requires them. ## Command-line arguments Programs started from a terminal can be given arguments: ```bash app hello 42 --verbose ``` `main` receives them through two parameters. ```cpp #include int main(int argc, char* argv[]) { std::cout << "Program: " << argv[0] << '\n'; for (int i{ 1 }; i < argc; ++i) { std::cout << "Argument " << i << ": " << argv[i] << '\n'; } return 0; } ``` | Parameter | Meaning | |---|---| | `argc` | "Argument count": how many there are, including the program's own name | | `argv` | "Argument vector": an array of C-strings ([[5.05 C-Style Arrays and C-Strings]]) | ``` argc is 4 argv[0] "app" argv[1] "hello" argv[2] "42" text, not a number argv[3] "--verbose" ``` Every argument arrives as text. Convert with `std::stoi(argv[2])` or `std::stod`, and always check `argc` before reading an index, since the user may have supplied fewer arguments than you expect. ## C-style variadic functions You may meet functions declared with `...`, which accept any number of arguments of any type: ```cpp double average(int count, ...); ``` The compiler checks neither the types nor the count, so mistakes become crashes. `printf` works this way. Modern C++ replaces it with `std::initializer_list`, `std::span` or variadic templates: [[9.03 Variadic Templates and Fold Expressions]]. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Declare a pointer `f` to a function that takes a `double` and returns `bool`. - `bool* f(double);` + `bool (*f)(double);` - `bool f*(double);` - `double (*f)(bool);` > The brackets around `*f` matter: `bool* f(double);` declares a function returning `bool*`. An alias such as `using Predicate = bool (*)(double);` reads more easily. ? Can a capturing lambda convert to a function pointer? - Yes, always - Yes, if it captures by reference + No, only a lambda that captures nothing can > A capturing lambda carries data, which a plain function pointer cannot hold. Use `std::function` or a template parameter instead. ? What is a callback? - A function that calls itself - A function that runs when the program ends + A function handed to other code, which calls it later - A function with a default argument > You hand the callback to other code, which calls it at the right moment, such as a comparison for sorting. ? What is in `argv[0]`? - The first argument the user typed - The number of arguments - Nothing; it is always empty + The name of the program itself > `argv[0]` is the program name. The user's arguments start at `argv[1]`, and `argc` counts them all. ```
ideas:
1. Write a calculator that uses a `switch` on `+ - * /` to choose a function pointer, then calls through it.
2. Make a `std::array<BinaryOp, 4>` of operations, loop over it and print each result for 8 and 2.
3. Write a program that prints its arguments and reports an error if none were given.

cards.q: Declare a pointer `f` to a function that takes a `double` and returns `bool`.
cards.a:
`bool (*f)(double);`

The brackets around `*f` matter: `bool* f(double);` declares a function returning `bool*`. An alias such as `using Predicate = bool (*)(double);` reads more easily.

cards.q: Can a capturing lambda convert to a function pointer?
cards.a:
No, only a lambda that captures nothing can

A capturing lambda carries data, which a plain function pointer cannot hold. Use `std::function` or a template parameter instead.

A function handed to other code, which calls it later

You hand the callback to other code, which calls it at the right moment, such as a comparison for sorting.

The name of the program itself

`argv[0]` is the program name. The user's arguments start at `argv[1]`, and `argc` counts them all.
